cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en My friend has Autism by Amanda Doring Turville, illustrated by Christian Sora. My name is Nick. This is my friend Zach. Zach and I belong to a model airplane club. Zach has autism. Airplanes are awesome. Zach likes building bwing planes. Fighter jets are my favorites. Zach knows a lot about airplanes. His nickname is pilot. I've learned more about planes from Zach than from anybody else. Sometimes Zach goes on and on about airplanes. Here piece the same facts over and over. It can seem like he's in his own world. Did you know kids with autism have trouble communicating? They may not talk much at all. They may talk only about their interests, even when other people don't share those interests. When Zach is focused on his models, he may not talk to me at all. We work on our own planes quietly or I'll tell him about my day. I feel like I can tell Zach anything. Did you know many kids with autism are able to focus very tightly on an interest? Zach and I play video games while we wait for the glue to dry. He's tough to beat. Sometimes I think he lets me win. Zach hears things most people don't hear. Loud noises can hurt his ears. On our field trip to the airport, he wore the coolest ear muffs ever. He looked like he worked there. Did you know many kids with autism may hear sounds or smell odors that other people don't notice? I wrestle with some of my other friends, but not with Zach. He feels things differently than most people. Zach doesn't like anybody touching him, not even to pin on his new wings. And that's okay. There are a lot of things I don't like, too. When I go to Zach's house, I bring my own models. It bothers Zach when other people touch or play with his models. Each plane has to be in just the right spot. Did you know kids with autism often spend a lot of time arranging toys or objects? It can upset them when somebody moves their things. Zach may not look at me while I'm talking to him. Sometimes he walks away. I know Zach doesn't mean to hurt my feelings. I just show them my new magazine some other time. Did you know many kids with autism can seem impolite? They don't understand that it's rude to walk away from someone who is talking to them. I'm really glad I met Zach. Of all my friends, Zach is the only one who likes model airplanes. It makes me feel good to be his friend. I know that he likes being my friend, too. What is autism? What is autism? Autism is a brain-based disorder. Doctors don't know what causes autism, and there is no cure. Kids with autism have trouble making sense of the world around them. They don't make connections with words and feelings like most people do. Kids with autism have trouble talking with others, which makes them hard to make friends. They often spend their time alone and seem to be in their own world. Therapy can help kids with autism communicate with others and live better lives. My friend Zach has a disability called autism, but that doesn't matter to us. We talk about airplanes, build models, and enjoy hanging out together. I'm glad Zach is my friend.

[screaming] Surya didn't think he was singing that loudly from his room. At least his big secret was safe for now. Surya liked to sing. Surya also liked to annoy his sister Deepa by singing while she practiced dance. Getting in trouble for annoying Deepa was one thing. But Surya worried about much bigger trouble. Yes, Surya liked to sing. But Surya loved to dance a hundred times more than he liked to sing. Surya wanted to dance Bharatanatyam Bharatanatyam more than anything. Bharatanatyam is a beautiful dance style where dancers use their whole bodies to create rhythmic movements and tell stories. Bharatanatyam comes from India where Surya's family is originally from. Surya liked to sound it out. Bha, ra, tha natyam. But he wanted to dance those movements even more. But Surya couldn't risk anybody finding out his love for dance. Surya had heard from his first grade friends at Bear Creek Elementary School that boys play sports. Boys don't dance. Ever. Even though Deepa had yelled at Surya for his boisterous singing, Surya risked a peek to watch her practice. He desperately wanted to learn the next steps in the dance. Surya peered around the family room corner to watch. But Deepa caught him. Amma! Surya is bothering me. He won't let me practice for the big dance recital. It's okay, Deepa, said a calm voice from upstairs. Surya watching isn't keeping you from practicing. Pretend like he's your audience. Just keep dancing. We have to leave for your rehearsal anyway. Come on, both of you. Time to go. Sighed Surya. Amma, his mom, came to his rescue. She got him out of trouble with Deepa, and she helped him keep his secret, even if she didn't realize it. Even better, Surya was going to the dance studio. Amma, Deepa, and Surya arrived at the Leela Dance Studio buzzing with a swarm of girls. Seeing all these girls remind Surya that boys aren't supposed to dance. The big recital was a week away. Each girl seemed electric with a mix of jitters and excitement. Even more thrilling, the dancers were elated about their costumes. Surya, you sit here and watch, okay? Said Amma. I'll be back after I help with the costumes for Deepa's group. Costume Deepa joined her teacher and classmates. Surya felt feelings of jealousy as he sat on the side like his Amma had told him to do. He watched eagerly, but he itched to get up and dance. The music started and the practice began. Deepa and her classmates performed each movement under Pooja Akkas, their teacher's watchful eye. She gently corrected mistakes and praised successes. The teacher's name was Pooja, but her students added Akka as a term of affection. It means older sister. Even though Pooja wasn't their actual older sister, Deepa and her classmates felt like she was. Surya had heard Deepa say these deep feelings of affection for her dance teacher are a special part of Indian culture. As Deepa and her classmates danced, no one noticed another dancer had joined the group. Surya couldn't help himself. Before Surya realized it, he had stood and joined the Bharatanatyam dance movements on the side in perfect unison with the class. All of a sudden, the music stopped. Surya was still dancing. It took him a moment before he realized everyone was now staring at him. Oh, no. What have I done? Surya wanted to escape from the studio, fast. His big secret was out. Deepa and his mom would be so mad. And the teacher, Pooja Akka, would be so annoyed. Surya had ruined their practice. Surya! Surya spun to run away, but froze in his tracks. He slowly turned and saw Pooja Akka gliding toward him. He braced for the worst. That was wonderful, Pooja Akka continued. What? Surya thought to himself. Surya was positive he'd be in trouble, big trouble. Instead, Pooja Akka praised him. She continued to smile at him brightly. Come to me, Surya. Please show me again. Surya didn't know what to do. Deepa's hands covered her gaping mouth, and her classmates were still staring. It's okay, Surya, Pooja Akka reassured. "I would love to see you try those movements again." Surya felt the whole room closing in. Not knowing what else to do, he slowly walked toward Pujakka. Her luminous eyes smiled with encouragement. Even before Pujakka could start the music, Surya began to dance and sing. He felt his fears melt away. Bharatanatyam had not done did that. Dance dispels Surya's fears. Maybe that's why Surya liked Bharatanatyam so much. Surya stamped and jumped to the melody and rhythms. He let his face show what he experienced. He practically glowed. Then, Pujakka giggled. Surya stopped and frowned. "It's okay, Surya. You're doing so well. You're shining like the sun. Just like the meaning of your name, Surya." Surya was relieved. Pujakka wasn't laughing at him. "But, you are doing everything on the opposite side, like a mirror image." Pujakka continued curiously. "Have you been watching Deepa dance from the front?" Mirror image? I haven't done anything wrong. Surya thought to himself dejected. Pujakka knelt next to him and whispered, "It's okay, Surya. This is easy to correct. Are you having fun?" It was as if she read his mind. Surya burst out, "I like to sing, but I really love to dance." He then said solemnly, "I know I'm not supposed to dance because I'm a boy." "Of course you're allowed to dance. Why do you think boys don't dance?" said Pooja Akka. Surya hesitated. "Do I tell her?" "Well, my friends at school told me only girls dance. And I've never seen a boy dance." "I see. Would you like to see something special, Surya? In fact, I think the whole class should see." Pooja Akka held Surya's hand as she led him over to where large photos hung on the wall. Why hadn't Surya noticed these before? Deepa and her classmates crowded around. "I want you all to see these photos of my teachers. Do you notice anything?" Surya couldn't believe it. One of the teachers was a man! The students gasped. "I didn't realize this!" one girl exclaimed. "This is one of my teachers, and he dances beautifully. His Bharatanatyam movements are magical. Boys are definitely allowed to dance if they want to, including you." Surya stood just a little taller and smiled a little wider. "Surya, if you want to learn, I will happily teach you. Being a girl or being a boy is not the most important part about dancing. Loving dance is the most important part of dancing." Surya's heart leaped to the sky. He would get to dance and not have to keep it a secret. But Surya still wasn't sure about the boys at his school. And some of the girls were looking at him funny. He scanned their faces. "My teacher had to prove himself," warned Pooja Akka. "You will, too. Do you think proving yourself is worth it?" "For dance, I will do it," Surya said with more courage than he felt. Amma, Surya and Deepa's mom, arrived just in time to see all of this unfold. Neither Amma nor Deepa was mad at Surya. No funny looks there. In fact, Amma uh beamed with tears of pride and joy. Deepa sprang over and gave Surya a big hug. "He's my brother, everyone! Surya, you should start learning so we can dance together next year's Bharatanatyam recital," exuded Deepa. "Maybe we can even do the talent show at school." "So, Surya, will I see you in class next time?" asked Pooja Akka. "Yes, I want to, Pooja Akka," said Surya as he grinned ear to ear. Surya was so excited, he didn't even bother to ask Amma. Once Deepa's classmates saw that Pooja Akka and Deepa approved, the class erupted in cheers. The car ride home overflowed with excitement. Amma and Deepa each told Surya how proud they were that he was going to learn Bharatanatyam. And then Deepa innocently said, "I can't wait to see what those silly boys at school think of you dancing." Surya went silent. His face drooped and his mood sank. He had forgotten all about his school friends who said boys don't dance. "What am I going to tell them? I guess I still have to keep this a secret." Monday morning rolled around. It was time for a new week of school. Surya's excitement from dance class turned to dread. "Maybe I should just change schools so I don't have to tell them," Surya thought to himself. Surya was so lost in his worries that he notice his friend Nicholas calling his name in the school hallway. "Surya, Surya, what did you do this weekend?" Before Surya knew it, he blurted out, "I accidentally danced in my sister's class." Gulp. Surya was ready to run. He was positive he'd have to change schools now. And Nicholas probably wouldn't be his friend much longer. Nicholas looked around and then whispered, "Oh, you dance, too?" "What?" Surya looked at Nicholas. "What do you mean, too?" Nicholas was still whispering. "I started tap dance class last year. My sister goes to ballet class, so my mom put me in tap class at the same time. I hated it at first, but after our recital, I realized dancing makes me happy, especially that click-clack of my tap shoes. I just couldn't tell anyone at school," Nicholas confided, "until now." Surya was shocked. Maybe boys dance after all. They just need to say it. "Nicholas, I don't know if our friends will make fun of us, but if we like to dance, we should say so," Surya exclaimed. Nicholas looked skeptical. Surya wasn't completely convinced, either, but it sounded good and felt right. And maybe those who said boys don't dance were few. Or maybe they just didn't understand. "Come on, Nicholas. We'll do this together." Nicholas nodded, and they gave each other a big thumbs-up. Surya wasn't sure how things would go with the other boys, but he felt a lot better knowing he wasn't alone. Don't forget to leave a review. >> Mhm.

Deepa LOVES to dance. She studies a dance from India called Bharatanatyam that is like moving poetry! But since her dance is different from what her friends at school do, she isn’t sure if she should share it. Should she? Will she?

cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en Dancing Deepa written by Suchi Sriram illustrated by Vinya Vasudevan. A new poster on the walls at Bear Creek Elementary School caught Deepa's eye. A talent show! Deepa enjoyed the excitement rising with dinner. But when Deepa looked more closely at the poster, her excitement drained away. The poster says, "Got talent? Audition." On the poster, Deepa saw pictures of singers, actors, musicians, martial artists, gymnasts, ballerinas, and tap dancers, even a unicyclist. But Deepa didn't see pictures of anyone dancing her kind of dance. A captivating dance from India called Bharatanatyam. It's a long word. Sound it out. Bha-ra-ta-na-tyam. You see, Deepa delights in dance. She wants to share dance with her whole school, the whole world even. The rhythms and expressions, the music and the costumes, Deepa cherished every element of Bharatanatyam. But she worried that her classmates wouldn't see Bharatanatyam that way. What if no one at Deepa's school would watch Bharatanatyam since it wasn't ballet or tap? What if her classmates didn't like the music? What if they thought her costume was too bright or even ugly? What if they decided she looked weird because of the facial expressions that go along with Bharatanatyam? Deepa thought teacher regularly insisted that all dance is beautiful. If you do it with love, Deepa certainly loved Bharatanatyam. But Deepa feared other students might laugh at the dance she loved or get bored or criticize it. Any of those would hurt too much. Deepa decided just forget auditioning for the talent show. The risk was too great. The next Wednesday was audition day. While Deepa chose to be happy for her friends who auditioned, she was disappointed she wouldn't get to dance. A few days later, several friends received the good news that they would be in the show. Deepa's classmate Anna, who studies ballet, said, "I am so excited, but I'm also nervous. I'm going to dance to music by Mozart. I love to dance because it makes me feel so happy." "I get that," Deepa said and smiled on the outside. At the same time, Deepa felt deeply wistful on the inside. She said to herself, "I love to dance, too. Anna and my friends don't even know I dance. Ballet is beautiful, but Bharatanatyam is too. Maybe I should do ballet instead. Then I could dance in the talent show." Talent show day arrived. The whole school buzzed with excitement. Deepa was fascinated by every act. If she liked each presentation this much, would these talented students like her Bharatanatyam? Deepa found the variety fascinating. She wouldn't have wanted to miss even one act. Deepa didn't know how many schoolmates excelled in such a wide assortment of activities. She's heard only a few speak of these interests before. Singers, dancers, actors, musician, even a magician. Deepa learned so much about each classmate. Despite each happy discovery, Deepa kept thinking, "I wish I could have danced, too." Deepa kept picturing herself dancing Bharatanatyam on stage. She heard the bells. Her face lit up with the expressions, but it was too late. Nobody would be watching her today. Deepa grew so distracted, confused that she just walked back to class after the show without saying a word. She forgot to congratulate those who performed. She didn't even talk to Anna, whose belly dance was exquisitely graceful. Deepa's fourth-grade teacher, Ms. Molina, was surprised to see Deepa leave that way. Ms. Molina found it even more worrisome that Deepa chose to sit alone, lost in her own thoughts. Deepa was friendly and usually showed deliberate interest in other students. "Is something bothering you, Deepa? Did you not like the show?" asked Ms. Molina. "Well," began Deepa, "I liked the show tremendously. Everyone did a great job, but "But what?" said Ms. Molina. "Would you like to talk about it?" Deepa hesitated. "Do I tell her? It'll sound so silly," she thought. But Ms. Molina had shown thoughtful kindness in the past. Deepa plunged ahead. "Well, I guess I wish I could have danced. I love to dance, but my dance is different. I wasn't sure if it was allowed or if anyone would like it. People might think my dance is weird or that I'm weird. Now, I'll never get a chance to dance in the talent show. Ms. Melina sat next to Deepa and said, "Anything that expresses your happiness and care can never be weird. Can you tell me more about your dance? I'd love to know more." Deepa's face lit up. "Really? You would? It's from India, where my whole family is from. The dance is called Bharatanatyam." "India? Oh, India is such a fascinating place with a very rich culture. I think students would love to learn more. I know I would. In fact, why don't you share something with the class on Monday?" Deepa froze. "The whole class? On Monday? This is exciting, but a little scary, too. What if they ask questions I can't answer?" At the same time, this was her big chance. Should she pass it up? "Yes, I'll do it," Deepa exclaimed. "Thank you, Ms. Melina." Deepa worked up her courage to ask Anna later that Friday if she would help her to change on Monday. She briefly told Anna about Bharatanatyam and what went into that costume. Deepa then explained, "Anna, since you are a dancer, you will know a few of the feelings I'm experiencing and how each piece of the costume needs to be just right." "I do get the feelings, Deepa, and of course I'll help you. Just tell me what to do." One classmate who hasn't laughed thought Deepa with relief. Deepa's teacher would be proud of her for taking a risk. Dancing for her class was the only thing Deepa could think about all weekend. On Saturday, Deepa excitedly told her dance teacher about her big opportunity. Deepa's dance teacher was over the moon proud of her for having the courage to share the dance she loved. "Why don't you start by telling them Bharatanatyam originated in India, then dance a piece. I'll let them ask questions. They will learn something from you and you will learn from their questions." "Learn from their questions?" Deepa thought. "Hmm, I don't know what she means, but I'll see what happens." Sunday was the longest day. Deepa's mind was a swirling soup of excitement, happiness, worry, and nervousness. She wondered how she could feel so many things at the same time. Finally, it was Monday, Deepa's big day to dance for her class. Just before class, Anna went with Deepa to the teacher's room next door, where Deepa put on her favorite Indian earrings and bangles, and changed into a red blouse and a blue Bharatanatyam, a long skirt. While Deepa changed, Anna said, "Take a deep breath, Deepa. That's what I do just before I dance, and it always helps me." Deepa breathed deeply and showed a wavering smile of thanks to Anna. She felt too nervous to speak. Anna said, "You're welcome, even if words are hard to say before a big performance." Finally, Deepa stuck a little round maroon bindi on her forehead with her finger. Saving the most special part for last, Deepa removed her shoes and attached her ankle bells so everyone could hear the rhythms in her feet. Ms. Melina announced, "Class, we have a delightful surprise today. I asked Deepa to share a little bit about a dance from India that she studies. She'll tell us a bit about Bharatanatyam, will dance it, and then we can ask her questions. Thump, thump, thump. Deepa's heart was racing. It's okay. It's okay. Just breathe. Just listen to the music. And dance. Music filled the classroom. Dum, dum, dum, dum. Deepa lifted her hands high above her head, gluing her palms together. She smiled brightly with her eyes and her lips as she danced, and stretched, and jumped, and turned to the rhythms and melody. Her ankle bells jingled with joy. Three minutes later, the class roared with cheers. How did you do all that at the same time? That looks so hard. I never knew dance would have so much facial expression. That is cool. How do you make your eyes and your neck do that? Those rhythms are so complicated. I don't really like dance very much, but I think I'd try that one. You did an amazing job. Don't your feet hurt by dancing barefoot? How do you keep smiling? Can you really tell stories dance without saying a word? Deepa couldn't believe it. Nobody thought she looked strange or danced weirdly. Classmates said they were tapping their toes to the music because it was catchy. Several said her costume was beautiful. Can you show us more? Yes, and next time, let's dance together. Ms. Molina nodded and smiled at Deepa. She said, "Thank you so much. This was even better than dancing in the school talent show." And smiled across the room, too. The end. >> Hey.
